transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-09
Start time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~64 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Raj (Redwood SE), Elena (Redwood), Lena (CTO, Solstice), Ben (ML Eng), Omar (Platform), Priya (Security)

[00:00] Maya: thanks everyone for taking the time. quick agenda: raj will walk through our prefix caching model, we'll dig into hit rates/key design, then discuss multi-tenant safety and private deployment implications.
[00:22] Lena: yup, excited — we've got a tight latency SLO for chat assist (p95 < 350ms) and want to understand if caching helps without opening security holes.
[00:34] Raj: cool. quick context from us: prefix/prompt caching (we sometimes call it KV or prefix cache) stores the transformer KV state for repeated prefixes, so you can skip recomputation for the beginning of a conversation or template. biggest wins when users have templated prompts or repeated system messages.
[01:05] Ben: our UI churns lots of similar system prompts across sessions — think 60% identical first 60 tokens. curious what hit rates you see.
[01:20] Raj: depends on product. templated assistant flows often hit 60-80%. general free-form chat is lower, 20-40%. for enterprise assistants with structured prompts, 40-60% is common. those numbers map to token savings but actual latency improvement also depends on KV cache locality and routing.
[01:45] Maya: note that hit rate is workload dependent — UX changes (small prompt edits) can drop effective hit rate, so we encourage caching on canonicalized templates where possible.
[02:05] Omar: what about cache keys — what's safe to include and how do we namespace per-tenant?
[02:15] Raj: our recommended key composition is always include immutable invariants: model_id|model_version|tokenizer_hash|prompt_template_id|tenant_id|prefix_hash. e.g. hash("gptx-3.1|v1|tok123|onboarding-welcome|tenant-abc|<prefix_text>"). The important part is model+tokenizer+tenant.
[02:45] Priya: do you ever include user_id? we have per-user personalization and some prompts are user-specific.
[02:55] Raj: you can include user_id but that's often handled with a higher-level namespace — including user_id is fine but reduces sharing and hit rate. we recommend 2-level keys for multi-tenant: tenant namespace + optional user namespace. also sign keys or put them behind auth tokens to avoid cache poisoning.
[03:25] Ben: what's cache poisoning in this context?
[03:30] Raj: if keys are predictable and someone can inject prefixes, they could cause valid cached KVs to be returned for a different prompt; signature+auth reduces that risk. also include prompt_template_id to avoid collisions between different templates that happen to share a prefix.
[03:50] Elena: on eviction and TTLs — how aggressive should teams be?
[03:56] Raj: tradeoff: longer TTL raises hit rates but increases memory usage. typical defaults: short-lived interactive caches 5-30 minutes, session-aware caches tied to session lifetime, and long-lived caches for static templates (hours). plus LRU eviction. we also enforce per-tenant memory caps to prevent noisy-tenant issues.
[04:30] Lena: multi-tenant safety — does Redwood Dedicated or Private give us stronger isolation?
[04:38] Raj: yes. hosted mode is multi-tenant at the service layer — we namespace aggressively and have quotas. Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity) provides dedicated GPU pools but still shared control plane, while Private/VPC can be single-tenant where caching is fully under your control. for regulated data we recommend Private with customer-managed networking and KMS.
[05:05] Priya: encryption at rest for the cache?
[05:08] Maya: private deployments can use customer KMS/HSM and disks are encrypted; hosted caches are encrypted at rest as part of our cloud provider contracts and keys are managed by us, but we can offer dedicated key options for enterprise contracts.
[05:30] Ben: compatibility — if we quantize a model or switch kernels, will the cached KV still be valid?
[05:38] Raj: short answer: KV cache is valid only across runs with the same exact model weights, tokenizer, and architecture. light compiler/kernel differences (optimizations) are fine if weights/tokenizer unchanged, but different quantization (e.g., 8-bit vs 4-bit) can change internal state shapes and may be incompatible. so we include quantization_profile or model_variant in cache key.
[06:05] Omar: interesting — that means when you fallback to cheaper quantized variant for cost, you can't always reuse cache from the full model.
[06:12] Raj: correct — we have strategies: pre-warm the quantized variant with a fast pass, or maintain side-by-side caches keyed by variant. tradeoffs are cost vs hit rate.
[06:30] Maya: another point: tokenization changes (like vocab merges) break caches — include tokenizer_hash as I mentioned.
[06:40] Lena: what about latency benefit numbers? does cache always help p95?
[06:45] Raj: prefix cache tends to give large speedups for the cached prefix portion. absolute p95 improvement depends on prefix length and backend routing. Example: 512-token prefix cached might reduce generation time by 30-70ms on a single step, but if the bulk of latency is model decode for new tokens, you'll still need batching/throughput tuning. If most requests are short, cache helps p95 a lot.
[07:20] Ben: batching — do we lose prefix-level benefits when batching many small requests?
[07:25] Raj: batching and caching complement each other. batch warm-up helps throughput; caching reduces per-request compute. However, if your routing sends cached hits to a fast cache path (no full model run) and uncached to GPU, you must ensure batching logic doesn't wait for cached responses, otherwise batching can add latency. we recommend separate fast-path for cache hits and async batching for misses.
[07:55] Priya: can cache be sharded across GPUs? we want to scale to big fleets.
[08:00] Raj: yes — cache is a sharded KV store with consistent hashing; shard placement respects tenant isolation policies. in private deployments, customers can pin shards to local nodes.
[08:18] Omar: operations — visibility/metrics we can expect?
[08:22] Elena: Console exposes token-level savings, per-key hit/miss rates, per-tenant memory usage, eviction rates, and latency breakdown (cache lookup vs model decode). We'll share a sample dashboard.
[08:40] Raj: also watch for hot-key patterns; very common prefixes can create imbalance — we recommend tiered caches (hot-cache + backing store) and rate limits to protect shared resources.
[09:05] Ben: examples of key hashing? show a sample config.
[09:10] Raj: sample: key = H("model=v1|tok=sha1|templ=onboard_v2|tenant=solstice|prefix_sha256"). We'll include config snippets in the doc. avoid using raw prompt text in the key unless you hash it.
[09:36] Maya: security note — never store PII in plaintext in cache keys. always hash or tokenize sensitively.
[09:45] Priya: good. what about testing and validating correctness? we need to be sure cached KVs don't change output semantics.
[09:52] Raj: recompute-based validation: for pilot, run A/B where cached path returns result and background recompute runs and diffs outputs; set acceptance thresholds. we can help with a harness that tags divergences.
[10:15] Lena: timeline & pilot?
[10:20] Maya: proposed pilot: 2-week experiment with 48-hour continuous benchmark plus 1 week of live shadowing. Raj will run bench using your sample prompts; we'll produce hit-rate projections and cost delta.
[10:35] Ben: sounds good. can you also note caveats around quantization / fallback?
[10:40] Raj: yes — we'll document variant-specific caches and fallback strategies (recompute on mismatch, or use warmed quantized caches).
[10:50] Maya: quick recap of action items and who does what (see action items).
[11:02] Lena: thanks all — Priya and I will review security docs when they arrive.
[11:08] Maya: great, we'll send the pack and follow up with scheduling.
[11:15] (meeting ends)

Notes: transcription contains minor speaker drift and a few autopct errors (e.g., "K V cache" shown in some lines). References shared: link to prefix caching doc (internal), sample dashboard screenshot (shared in chat), benchmark spreadsheet (will be shared).
